raw_md:
# META (Meta Platforms, Inc.) — Value Investor Note

## Circle of Competence
Easy to understand at the model level: Meta sells attention. Billions of daily users across Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp, and Messenger generate engagement; Meta auctions targeted ad inventory against that engagement; advertisers pay for measurable outcomes. No exotic financial engineering. The genuine competence-stretching question is Reality Labs and the AI infrastructure supercycle — whether tens of billions a year in AI/datacenter capex is a rational extension of the core moat (better ranking, better ad targeting, new surfaces like Meta AI) or an empire-building distraction. That is a live, unresolved debate, not a settled fact, and it is the reason this stock is down double digits over the last year despite a genuinely excellent core business.

## Moat & Durability — Score 8/10
Network effects at Meta's scale (Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp, Messenger) are about as durable a moat as exists in consumer tech: users draw advertisers, ad revenue funds the product investment that keeps users, and the data advantage from that scale (second only to Google in breadth) lets Meta monetize attention more efficiently than smaller rivals. 81.7% gross margins and 34.8% operating margins are the receipts — this is genuine, structural pricing power, not a temporary window. The moat is under real, not hypothetical, pressure on two fronts: TikTok has proven attention can migrate to a rival platform, especially among younger cohorts, and privacy regulation (App Tracking Transparency already cost Meta real revenue once; further regimes could recur) can blunt targeting precision faster than Meta can rebuild around it. Reality Labs is a persistent multi-billion-dollar annual drag with no proven return, which is why this is an 8 and not a 9 or 10.

## Management & Capital Allocation
A 29.8% ROE on moderate leverage (debt/equity ~43%, predominantly bond-funded infrastructure debt rather than distress borrowing) implies the core ads business remains an efficient capital compounder. What the numbers can't confirm from this packet: buyback pace, insider selling patterns, or M&A discipline. The structural flag Munger would raise immediately is governance — Zuckerberg's dual-class super-voting shares mean outside shareholders have no real check on capital allocation, and the sustained, multi-year Reality Labs losses (tens of billions cumulatively) are effectively a founder's personal conviction bet that the market never got a vote on. His own large economic stake keeps incentives roughly aligned, but 'trustworthy' here means 'skilled and economically aligned,' not 'accountable to shareholders in the normal sense.'

The clearest capital-allocation tell in this packet is the free-cash-flow yield of just 1.4% against a P/E-implied earnings yield near 4.5% (1/22.4). That ~3-point gap is almost entirely the AI/datacenter capex supercycle being expensed through cash flow rather than the income statement's depreciation schedule. Whether that capex is high-return growth investment or over-building is the single question that determines whether this is a great capital allocation story or a cautionary one — and it cannot be answered from fundamentals alone.

## Predictability
The core ads auction has historically been one of the most predictable, highest-margin machines in public markets, but the momentum data here show a market that is actively re-pricing the AI-capex question rather than treating the story as settled: -23.7% over 12 months, -10.7% in the last month, -8.5% over six months, price still -5.3% below the 200-day moving average, RSI a neutral 49.9. That is real volatility around a real open question, not noise. Revenue growth of 28% is genuinely strong and argues the top-line story remains intact; the uncertainty is entirely about what falls to owner earnings after the AI infrastructure bill. No momentum thesis was populated in the packet, so there's no additional qualitative signal here beyond the price action itself. This fails Munger's 'easy decision' bar — a real judgment call is required, not a rubber stamp.

## Inversion — How an Owner Loses Money From Here
1. **Capex outruns monetization**: AI/datacenter spend keeps compounding faster than incremental ad revenue, ad-load, or new product revenue (Meta AI, business messaging) can offset it, permanently depressing free cash flow and ROIC even as the reported income statement still looks fine for a while.
2. **Regulatory impairment of the targeting engine**: antitrust remedies, a forced structural change, or privacy/ad-targeting restrictions spreading to new jurisdictions blunt the precision-targeting advantage that underwrites Meta's premium ad pricing — this has happened once (ATT) and could happen again.
3. **Attention migration outruns the AI payoff**: users, especially younger cohorts, keep shifting engagement to TikTok or the next platform faster than Reality Labs or Meta AI mature into revenue, eroding the core engagement base the entire ad-auction economy depends on.

## Valuation
The packet gives market cap ($1.503T), trailing P/E (22.4x), forward P/E (16.9x), FCF yield (1.4%), and ROE (29.8%) but not share count or share price directly. Backing into per-share terms using an approximate ~2.5B diluted share count (a modeling assumption, not sourced from the packet) implies a current price near $601/share, trailing EPS near $26.81, forward EPS near $35.55, and FCF/share near $8.62 — a striking gap between accounting earnings and cash owner earnings, driven by the AI capex supercycle.

Normalizing owner earnings between the depressed reported FCF/share ($8.62, likely too conservative because much of the capex is growth rather than pure maintenance) and trailing EPS/share ($26.81, likely too generous because it doesn't fully capture the cash cost of the buildout), a starting owner-earnings estimate of roughly $18–$21/share seems reasonable.

Two-stage owner-earnings DCF:
- **Low case** ($18/share starting owner earnings, 8% growth for 5 years fading to 2.5% terminal, 10% discount rate reflecting real capex/regulatory risk): ~$310/share.
- **High case** ($21/share starting owner earnings, 12% growth for 5 years fading to 3.5% terminal, 9% discount rate if AI capex converts efficiently into monetizable products): ~$570/share.

Midpoint ~$440/share vs. an implied current price of ~$601/share gives a margin of safety of roughly **-26.8%** — the market is charging a premium to normalized owner earnings, not offering a discount. That premium is arguably earned by the moat quality and growth rate, but it leaves very little room for the AI capex bet to disappoint, which is exactly the risk the 12-month -23.7% drawdown is pricing.

## The Cloning Caveat
The roster here is unusually strong and unusually large: Clifford Sosin (CAS Investment Partners, a highly concentrated manager) opened a new position at 4.08% of portfolio; Lee Ainslie (Maverick Capital) opened new at 3.88%; Daniel Loeb (Third Point) opened new at 2.47%; David Tepper (Appaloosa) added 54.6% to reach 1.8%; Viking Global both opened new and then added again (75.8% increase) across two quarters; Bill Ackman (Pershing Square) added 20.1%. Deep-value shops corroborate too — Bill Nygren (Oakmark), Dodge & Cox, Glenn Greenberg (Brave Warrior, a concentrated value investor), and Robert Vinall (RV Capital) are all adding. This is a genuinely broad convergence of both concentrated growth-oriented and classic value investors on the name after a real drawdown, which is meaningful corroboration — several of these are real, sized positions (4%+) from managers who don't buy baskets. It is still corroboration, not a substitute for the valuation work: the size and quality of this buying supports the moat and predictability read, but it does not resolve the core question of whether today's price already assumes the AI capex pays off.

## Verdict
**Watch, conviction 5/10.** This is a wonderful, understandable business with one of the strongest network-effect moats available at this scale, run by a skilled if unaccountable capital allocator, going through a real and reasonable market re-rating around AI capex intensity. The valuation work here says the current price already sits above the midpoint of a defensible normalized-owner-earnings range (implied ~-27% margin of safety), which fails the sensible-price checklist item even with a durable moat and a strong superinvestor roster. The right move is patience: this is a name to own at a better price, not to chase at today's price on moat quality and manager conviction alone.
momentum_thesis: META's price momentum is broken across every window — 1m -10.7%, 3m -3.9%, 6m -8.5%, 12m -23.7% — and the shape matters more than the levels: the 1-month return is worse than the 3-month, meaning the tape took a fresh leg down in just the last few weeks rather than grinding out a stable base, and the stock still sits 5.3% below its 200DMA with RSI14 pinned at 49.9 — dead neutral, no oversold spring loaded. Short interest is negligible (1.43% of float, 1.55 days to cover), so there's no squeeze fuel underneath this name; any rally has to be built on fresh buying, not shorts capitulating. The one genuinely bullish technical signal is options positioning — a put/call OI ratio of 0.49 skews call-heavy, which diverges from the negative spot trend and suggests derivatives desks aren't pricing further downside with conviction. Layered on top is an unusually broad and persistent superinvestor bid: Sosin, Ainslie, Loeb, Viking and Dodge & Cox all initiated new positions across Q1-Q2 2026, and rather than being one-off dip buys, several re-upped hard into the weakness — Viking added another 75.8% on top of its new position, Tepper +54.6%, Ackman +20.1%, Dorsey +23.6% — which reads as conviction accumulation through a drawdown, not a single capitulation-buy. Net: this is a fundamentals-driven, multi-manager accumulation story riding on top of a still-deteriorating price trend, not a name with its own technical tailwind yet.
